# ‘Seaweed could power Nigeria’s food production’

![](https://cdn.thenationonlineng.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/07191702/SMEFUNDS-Dr.-Femi-Oye.webp)

Seaweed, long associated with coastal communities elsewhere in the world, could become a source of clean energy for farmers and food processors in [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria), Chief Executive, SMEFUNDS, Dr Femi Oye has said.

He said his organisation has been exploring alternative energy sources to support economic activity across the country, including solar-powered household devices, and sees seaweed as a promising addition to the mix.

“Energy cost is one of the biggest burdens on small businesses in food production, from irrigation and drying to cold storage and processing. We have been looking at solar-powered household devices and other alternatives, and seaweed is one resource that deserves serious attention,” Oye said.

Seaweed grows quickly without farmland, fresh water or fertiliser, which makes it attractive as a renewable feedstock. Elsewhere, it has been used to produce biogas and biofuels, while the residue left after processing can serve as a natural fertiliser or an ingredient in animal and fish feed. For a country with a long Atlantic coastline and extensive creeks and lagoons, that combination of energy and farm inputs could be significant.

Oye said the greatest promise lies in a circular approach, in which nothing is wasted. “If seaweed can generate energy and the by-products can feed our soils and our fish ponds, then we are not just solving one problem. We are building a system where each output becomes another producer’s input,” he said.

He pointed to growing global interest in turning underused biological resources into commercially useful products, such as recovering proteins and oils from seafood by-products for aquaculture feed, as evidence that circular models can work when properly tested and scaled.

Oye cautioned that seaweed energy in Nigeria is at an early stage and will need careful study before it can be rolled out. “We must be realistic. We need pilot projects, technical research and the right partners to understand which species will thrive in our waters and what it will cost to produce energy at scale.But the potential is too important to ignore,” he said.

He called on government agencies, research institutions, investors and coastal communities to collaborate on pilot schemes, adding that small and medium-sized enterprises must be at the centre of any such effort. “If this is going to work, it must work for the small processor, the fish farmer and the household, not only for large industry,” he said.

Oye said SMEFUNDS will continue to back innovations that lower energy costs and improve productivity. “Our goal is simple: to make it easier and cheaper for Nigerians to produce food and grow their businesses,” he said.
